overview: Five dynasties of Turkic and Afghan sultans ruled from Delhi from 1206 to 1526, at their height under the Khaljis and Tughluqs reaching the far south. They brought Persian letters, Islamic architecture and Sufi shrines to northern India, and their India shaped the Mughals.

items.text: The Qutb Minar was begun under Qutb al-Din Aibak and finished by Iltutmish; at 72.5 meters it is the tallest brick minaret in the world.
The true arch and dome arrived with the sultanate; the Alai Darwaza of 1311 is the first building in India built entirely on those principles.
Amir Khusrau of Delhi wrote Persian verse and is credited with the beginnings of Hindustani music and poetry.
Chishti Sufis such as Nizamuddin Auliya drew Hindus and Muslims alike to their shrines and their music.
Persian was the language of court and chancery, and Indo-Persian history writing began with Minhaj-i Siraj and Barani.
Alauddin Khalji fixed market prices and had the land measured for revenue; paper and the spinning wheel spread through India in these centuries.
Persian wheels lifted water for irrigation.
Indo-Islamic culture and the Persian chancery passed to the Mughals.
The Qutb Minar and its monuments were listed by UNESCO.

fall.text: Babur's guns and cavalry defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in April 1526, and the Mughal Empire began.

sources.title: UNESCO, Qutb Minar and its Monuments, Delhi
